introduction: “The recognition of others shall not serve as proof for thee, nor shall the rejection of all else stand as evidence against thee.” The first half of these readings makes each person answerable for his own understanding: God gave reason so that people would not imitate, and at the last each soul is questioned “upon his own understanding.” The second half faces what follows. If everyone sees for himself, people will see differently, and Bahá’u’lláh explains why: souls have different capacities, and each mirror reports what is within itself. The Báb describes two believers each condemning the other from the same scripture. The conclusion is ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s: those who understand a station differently “should not interfere with” one another. Paul reached the same place over the disputes of his churches, and the Talmud, the Buddha and the parable of the elephant account for differing views much as the readings do. Two passages ask the question from the other side: a letter of Peter’s warns against private interpretation, and Paul elsewhere wants everyone to “speak the same thing.”
questions: “The Lord questioneth each soul upon his own understanding.” What follows for how you hold a belief you have never examined?
“The differences in the forms of mirrors.” Recall a disagreement about a sacred text. What in each reader shaped what each saw?
Two believers quote the same scripture against each other. What does the Báb say of both?
Is every understanding as good as another? What do the readings, and the warning against “private interpretation,” suggest?
“These various schools should not interfere with” one another. What makes that hard when the matter is one you care about most?

outside.why: God “has created in man the power of reason, whereby man is enabled to investigate reality.” Paul: prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
The seeker must “hear with the ear of God and see with” his own eye. Whitman: you shall no longer take things at second or third hand; you shall listen to all sides and filter them from your self.

By the aid of justice “thou shalt see with thine own eyes and not through the eyes of others.” The Qur’án: follow not that whereof thou hast no knowledge. Lo! the hearing and the sight and the heart, of each of these it will be asked.
“Every soul must ponder what hath been revealed and search with their own intellect.” The Bereans: they searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
Each must draw near “by themselves and of their own accord.” The Samaritans: now we believe, not because of thy saying: for we have heard him ourselves.
“The recognition of others shall not serve as proof for thee.” Paul, on a question that divided his churches: let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind.
“Ye have ever been responsible unto your own selves.” The Qur’án: no burdened soul can bear another’s burden.
The Lord questions each soul “upon his own understanding, not upon his subservience to the opinions of another.” Paul: every one of us shall give account of himself to God.

A New Testament letter warns: no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation. If each soul answers for its own understanding, what keeps understanding from becoming merely private? What do the readings offer as a check?
“The light is the light no matter from what lamp it” shines. Kabír: from the One Light, the entire universe welled up. So, who is good, and who is bad?

Each takes from the ocean what his cup will hold. The Talmud on why honest readers differ: as a hammer breaks a stone into several fragments, so one verse is stated by God and from it emerge several explanations.

“The root of all differences … stems from the differences in the forms of mirrors. Each one relates … what exists within itself.” The blind men and the elephant: each was partly in the right, and all were in the wrong.
Paul on the mirror every reader looks into: now we see through a glass, darkly; now I know in part.
One calls the other extremist, the other calls him rejecter, both quoting the word of God. The Buddha: they quarrel and fight, people seeing one side.

“We have created souls with different capacities.” Paul on believers of different strength: let not him that eateth despise him that eateth not; and let not him which eateth not judge him that eateth.
Those who hold different views of Christ’s station “should not interfere with” one another. A maxim from the wars of religion: in essentials unity, in non-essentials liberty, in all things charity.

Paul could also write: that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you; perfectly joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment. How can a community have one mind and many understandings?

romans-fully-persuaded-in-his-own-mind.text: One man esteemeth one day above another: another esteemeth every day alike. Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind
